title: The Walk Away from Racial Equality
affiliations: Florida A&M University College of Law

detail.title: The Walk Away from Racial Equality

publicationDetails.detailsText: 20 Northwestern Journal of Law and Social Policy 1 (2025) (Lead article).

detail.abstract:
This article demonstrates that the U.S. Supreme Court has walked away from racial equality in favor of the same liberal equality approach that was the foundation for Plessy v. Ferguson’s “separate but equal” doctrine. The Court’s recent affirmative action cases, from Grutter and Gratz v. Bollinger, to Fisher v. University of Texas, to Students for Fair Admissions v. President and Fellows of Harvard College, all apply a liberal equality theory that is hostile to racial equality. In the lead-up to these cases, the Court abandoned its Brown-era interpretation of equality under the Fourteenth Amendment Equal Protection Clause in favor of a liberty-centered jurisprudence that is essentially a reapplication of the Plessy-era theory of equality. Under the Plessy-era liberal equality framework, Fourteenth Amendment equality does not require positive action to advance full racial inclusion so long as law and government action provides for the same facilities for all. This “sameness” approach is the essence of the liberal component to liberal equality. Today, liberal equality is the theoretical foundation for affirmative action decisions, based on the idea that the use of race should always be subject to the strictest scrutiny even when that use is intended to benefit racial minorities.

This article distinguishes racial equality from liberal equality. It addresses how the Burger Court began the transition away from a racial equality-based doctrine, which has led to the point we are today with a re-embrace of Plessy-era liberal equality under Students for Fair Admissions. Ignoring the white supremacy concerns that underlie foundational Equal Protection Clause decisions like Loving v. Virginia, and instead focusing exclusively on differential treatment or discrimination concerns, removes a core component to the meaning of equal protection. Equality as identical treatment is only half the story; the other half is racial equality – the end of racialized hierarchy.

detail.abstract: The artificial intelligence industry is experiencing an unprecedented economic transformation characterized by simultaneous market consolidation and growth-a phenomenon we term "dual-phase market evolution." This paper analyzes the structural economic challenges facing AI companies, particularly the unsustainable unit economics that plague consumer-facing applications, while examining the emergence of viable business models in specialized enterprise applications. Through analysis of current market dynamics, venture capital flows, and technological governance patterns, we identify three distinct economic scenarios that will shape the industry's future: price normalization, cost collapse, and selective market consolidation. Our findings suggest that while venture-subsidized horizontal platforms face extinction, specialized vertical applications serving regulated industries demonstrate sustainable competitive advantages. This research contributes to understanding technology adoption patterns, economic sustainability in emerging industries, and the role of governance frameworks in technology maturation.

detail.title: Digital Finance and the Synergy of Pollution Control and Carbon Reduction From Dual Heterogeneity Perspective: A Geographically Weighted Quantile Regression Model
detail.abstract: Digital finance has great potential in promoting the synergy of pollution control and carbon reduction (PCCR). However, the spatial heterogeneity and response heterogeneity of digital finance on the synergy of PCCR remain underexplored. This study employs local spatial autocorrelation analysis and kernel density estimation to examine the spatial patterns of synergistic effect (SE1) and synergistic efficiency (SE2) across 2335 Chinese counties in 2022. Subsequently, this study applies the cutting-edge geographically weighted quantile regression (GWQR) model to investigate the spatial and response heterogeneity of digital finance's impact on SE1 and SE2. The study showed that SE1 generally decreases from eastern to western China, whereas SE2 exhibits a decline from central-western regions toward the east. Digital finance consistently enhances both SE1 and SE2, thereby strengthening integrated pollutant management. In terms of spatial heterogeneity, the positive impact of digital finance on SE1 weakens gradually from east to west, while its effect on SE2 strengthens gradually from east to west. Regarding response heterogeneity, the positive impacts on both SE1 and SE2 increase progressively with rising quantiles, with over 98% of coefficients showing statistically positive associations. The robustness of the conclusions is further validated using quantile regression and geographically weighted regression models.

title: The Myth of Credit Card Competition
affiliations: Vanderbilt University - Vanderbilt Law School

detail.title: The Myth of Credit Card Competition
detail.abstract:
You pay an invisible tax every time you swipe your credit card to pay—whether to buy groceries, grab a coffee, or access transportation.  Credit card companies charge merchants to process your transaction, who in turn increase their own prices.  These swipe fees are both extractive—higher than the cost of service and the fees in most other countries—and regressive—placing more of the cost burden on lower-income consumers and smaller merchants.  Such outcomes are typically associated with firms having material market power.  Yet, this market has competition: Consumers choose various cards offered by multiple card issuers, including banks and networks like American Express, Discover, Mastercard, and Visa.  Nevertheless, these problems persist.

The consensus treats these poor outcomes as the result of an imperfect market.  If merchants could better price their products to reflect the costs of different card payments or if additional networks existed, then prices would fall and price discrimination would dissipate.  This Article challenges the view that increasing competition is the proper antidote.  This view ignores how this market is structured.  Issuers of cards are incentivized to raise swipe fees to fund more generous rewards to attract more cardholders to use their cards.  In doing so, issuers channel rewards-focused consumers to merchants who take their cards.  Merchants incur this fee, rather than surcharge or reject these cards, to avoid dissuading credit-card users from spending at their stores.

This Article argues that a better answer can be found in public utility law, which requires rates to be just and reasonable and forbids rate discrimination.  Rate regulation, while out of vogue today, has long facilitated affordable and broad access to payments infrastructure, including for checks and debit cards.  Using credit cards as a lens, this Article shows how only using rate regulation for natural monopolies is too narrow and requires reconsideration.

detail.abstract: This article examines the types of crypto-asset risks that EU banks can prudently take under the transitional regulatory regime introduced by Article 501d of CRR3 and supplemented by the EBA's draft regulatory technical standards (RTS). The analysis is grounded in the evolving EU legal framework, particularly MiCAR and CRR3, and considers how banks may engage with crypto-assets through custody, payments and trading, and issuance. detail.abstract:
Under common law, tax statutes had, for a long time, been interpreted through a strict constructionist approach, with occasional departures and limited exceptions. This approach to interpretation barred the courts from going further to look for extrinsic materials for use in determining the purpose of the provisions. The fact that taxpayers kept inventing new schemes for tax avoidance led to the rise of purposive interpretation.

This paper begins with a brief outlook of Kenya’s judicial philosophy in interpretation of tax statutes. It points out that Kenyan courts have appreciated and embraced the fact that tax statutes ought to be construed through the traditional strict approach. The second part of this paper then reveals a contradictory approach from a keen reading of some of the authorities from the Court of Appeal. It argues that whereas courts label their canon of interpretation as strict construction, some of their decisions tend to lean towards purposive interpretation. This signifies a subtle trend towards purposive interpretation in Kenya.

The third part of this paper then turns to the influence that the Base Erosion and Profit Shifting (BEPS) project at the international stage could have on the choice of mode of interpretation. It argues that the solutions contained therein provide for anti-avoidance rules that invite purposive interpretation. Further, that implementation of BEPS reforms will lead to an increased use of the General Anti-Avoidance Rule under Section 23 of the Income Tax Act, which itself calls for purposive interpretation. 

The paper concludes by observing that the time is ripe for Kenyan courts to unite tax statutes with other statutes. It points out that as taxpayers get more complicated, holding on to literal interpretation may be more detrimental than beneficial.

detail.abstract: We investigate the hypothesis that relational and emotional intelligence are critical determinants of subjective wellbeing-both cognitive (life satisfaction) and eudaimonic (sense of meaning)-due to their central role in solving social dilemmas and managing the interplay between emotional and rational decision-making processes. We conceptualize and construct composite indices for relational and emotional intelligence and empirically test their associations with subjective wellbeing using multivariate econometric models, while also addressing the non-random income non-response bias with a sufficient condition methodology. Our findings reveal that both relational and emotional intelligence are positively and significantly associated with life satisfaction and life meaning, with only a few exceptions. We demonstrate that, under plausible parametric assumptions, these associations are strong enough to constitute sufficient conditions for subjective wellbeing. Specifically, the probability of reporting high life satisfaction increases substantially-by over 20%-with higher emotional intelligence, while both forms of intelligence exhibit strong predictive power for experiencing a strong sense of life purpose. The robustness of our results is confirmed across alternative model specifications and addressing further the endogeneity problem with a generalised structural equation model using valid instrument. These results suggest that investments in soft skills-often undervalued relative to cognitive competencies-have substantial implications for personal wellbeing and social cohesion. Our study provides empirical support for integrating relational and emotional intelligence development into educational curricula, workforce training, and public health strategies aimed at promoting holistic wellbeing.

title: From Open Banking to Banking-as-a-Service: Regulatory Challenges in the Evolution of Financial Intermediation

detail.title: From Open Banking to Banking-as-a-Service: Regulatory Challenges in the Evolution of Financial Intermediation

publicationDetails.detailsText: Singapore Management University School of Law Research Paper Forthcoming
publicationDetails.journalName: Singapore Management University Yong Pung How School of Law Legal Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Over the past decade, financial innovation has moved from open banking, centred on consumer-permissioned data sharing, to banking-as-a-service (BaaS), which modularizes core banking functions through application programming interfaces. This shift allows fintechs and non-financial platforms to embed financial products seamlessly, reducing transaction costs and fostering innovation. Yet the 2024 collapse of Synapse in the United States exposed the fragility of this model when intermediaries operate outside robust oversight, leaving consumers without recourse and revealing liability fragmentation and regulatory blind spots. This paper distinguishes BaaS from open banking, open finance, and embedded finance, and maps leading global models-from bank-led infrastructures to middleware providers and BigTech ecosystems. A comparative review of the EU, UK, US, Singapore, and China shows that open banking regimes remain inadequate for the risks of functional unbundling. The article proposes a regulatory model centred on licensing, liability clarity, resilience, prudential standards, and systemic safeguards.

title: Sino-AI: AI Regulations in Sinophone Regions
affiliations: Harvard University - Harvard Law School

detail.title: Sino-AI: AI Regulations in Sinophone Regions
detail.abstract: China's rise as an AI power challenges the narrative in the U.S. and increasingly in Europe that innovation is stifled by excessive regulation, because China has a robust AI regulatory regime that prohibits a wide range of AI applications and activities that imperil public safety. At the same time, most people live in countries that do not realistically aspire to become pioneers in either AI technology or AI regulations. For these countries, the question of whether innovation in AI is hindered by regulation is not as urgent because these countries are unlikely to ever become AI leaders in any case. Moreover, strict regulations of AI services would be difficult to enforce for most countries that lack the regulatory capacity and experience of jurisdictions like China or the EU. Finally, since AI models have become quite popular among the general public, most governments have been reluctant to restrict access to these models for fear of a public backlash. Thus, this paper takes a closer look at three notable "Sinophone" regions and "middle powers" outside of Mainland China, namely Taiwan, Singapore, and Hong Kong, to examine how their approaches to AI regulation have been influenced by their desire to balance innovation with risk mitigation in light of their limitations as "middle powers."

title: Improving Tax Compliance among the Clients of Tax Preparers
affiliations: University of Maryland, McCourt School of Public Policy; Georgetown University, American University, University of Warwick and Georgetown University

detail.title: Improving Tax Compliance among the Clients of Tax Preparers
detail.abstract: Faced with the complexity of the U.S. tax system, many taxpayers use tax preparers to complete their returns. These taxpayers file a disproportionate share of tax returns that overclaim refundable tax credits. We report on a randomized evaluation testing the efficacy of two versions of a letter sent by the Internal Revenue Service to taxpayers who used a preparer who likely made errors on their returns and filed a large number of returns containing probable filing errors, such as overclaiming tax credits. Both versions improve voluntary tax compliance, increasing the likelihood that recipients change their filing method by 19% and generating taxpayer savings of approximately $15.2 million. Sending the letters induced a large spillover effect on taxpayers who were not sent a letter but who used a tax preparer who had other clients sent letters, equaling approximately 40% of the size of the main effect of the letter.

title: Personalized By AI, Shared By Me: Promoting Brand Relationships In E-Business
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and Universidad Pública de Navarra

detail.title: Personalized By AI, Shared By Me: Promoting Brand Relationships In E-Business
detail.abstract: With the rise of digitalization and technological advancements, online streaming services are increasingly implementing AI to deliver highly personalized content, thereby enhancing the customer experience. As individuals frequently share personal information with others, we explore the consequences of socially sharing AI-generated content on social media. Specifically, we examine the actual sharing behavior of AI-personalized content and how posting such content increases brand loyalty. Moreover, we identify brand warmth as a key mediating mechanism. Our findings suggest that emotional perceptions, not competence, drive the link between sharing and loyalty. Additionally, sharing AI-generated content enhances one’s sense of authenticity. Thus, we recommend that managers provide consumers with personalized AI-generated content and encourage them to share it on social media to elicit more favorable consumer responses. The research reinforces the broad relevance of social sharing in strengthening consumer-company relationships, even when the content originates from a non-human, data-driven source. Therefore, this study advances theoretical discussions at the intersection of AI, digital commerce, communication, and consumer behavior within the digital music industry.

title: Efectividad de la política monetaria y elasticidad precio de la oferta de la vivienda en una economía emergente (Monetary Policy Effectiveness and Price Elasticity of Housing Supply in an Emerging Economy)
affiliations: Central Bank of Colombia and

detail.title: Efectividad de la política monetaria y elasticidad precio de la oferta de la vivienda en una economía emergente (Monetary Policy Effectiveness and Price Elasticity of Housing Supply in an Emerging Economy)
detail.abstract:
Spanish abstract: La elasticidad precio de la oferta en el mercado de vivienda es determinante a la hora de establecer el efecto de un choque de demanda agregada, como puede ser un choque de política monetaria, sobre la variación de los precios de la vivienda. Estudios de este tipo han sido realizados principalmente para economías avanzadas, pero para economías emergentes, como la colombiana, los estudios son escasos. En este documento hacemos una estimación de dicha elasticidad oferta utilizando información a nivel de ciudades de Colombia y con una metodología econométrica de parámetros variantes en el tiempo para el período 2011T2-2024T4. Adicionalmente, estimamos el efecto de un choque de política monetaria sobre los precios de la vivienda dependiendo del nivel de elasticidad oferta de esta. Nuestros hallazgos muestran que para todas las ciudades la elasticidad oferta fue decreciente hasta antes de la pandemia de COVID-19, que durante esta se incrementó y posteriormente volvió a ser decreciente. Para ciudades como Bogotá, la elasticidad osciló entre 4,7% y 9,9% y para ciudades como Armenia estuvo entre 14,8% y 22,4%. Por su parte, teniendo en cuenta esta heterogeneidad entre ciudades, estimamos que un aumento unitario en la sorpresa de política monetaria tiene un efecto fuerte y duradero de reducción de 6 pp del crecimiento de los precios de la vivienda a medida que la curva de oferta se torna más inelástica. La tendencia decreciente de la elasticidad oferta en el tiempo está relacionada con el aumento de la población en las ciudades.

English abstract: The price elasticity of supply in the housing market is crucial when determining the effect of an aggregate demand shock, such as a monetary policy shock, on the variation in housing prices. Studies of this type have been conducted mainly for advanced economies, but for emerging economies, like Colombia, such studies are scarce. In this paper, we estimate this supply elasticity using city-level data from Colombia and a time-varying parameter econometric methodology for the period 2011Q2 - 2024Q4. Additionally, we estimate the effect of a monetary policy shock on housing prices depending on the level of supply elasticity. Our findings show that for all cities, supply elasticity was decreasing until before the COVID-19 pandemic, then increased during the pandemic and subsequently decreased again. For cities like Bogotá, the elasticity ranged from 4.7% to 9.9%, and for cities like Armenia, it ranged from 14.8% to 22.4%. Taking into account this heterogeneity across cities, we estimate that a unitary increase in the monetary policy surprise has a strong and lasting effect, reducing house price growth by 6 pp as the supply curve becomes more inelastic. The decreasing trend of housing elasticities over time is related to the increase in cities population.

title: THE ROLE OF SOCIAL NETWORKING SITES IN SHAPING RECRUITMENT STRATEGIES AND APPLICANT INTENT
affiliations: University of Valencia and Universidad de Valencia

detail.title: THE ROLE OF SOCIAL NETWORKING SITES IN SHAPING RECRUITMENT STRATEGIES AND APPLICANT INTENT
detail.abstract: This article explores the role and impact of social networking sites (professional and non-professional) in recruitment. Specifically, the influence of information quality, trustworthiness, effectiveness, and perceived ease of use on the quality of two social networking sites (LinkedIn and Facebook). The results with 200 individuals over 21 years old show that the four variables positively influence the quality of social networking sites and that there is a positive relationship between the quality of social networking sites and intent to apply. From a managerial perspective, the results gathered from this study help employers identify which SNS is best to post their career openings and focus on their recruitment strategy. From an academic perspective, the data from this research provides insight into how SNSs can be incorporated into recruitment marketing strategies.

title: The Visual Dimension of E-Commerce: How Do Product Images Shape Online Purchase Decisions?
affiliations: Korea University Business School and Korea University Business School

detail.title: The Visual Dimension of E-Commerce: How Do Product Images Shape Online Purchase Decisions?
detail.abstract: The uncertainty of product quality is a major challenge in online retail, where consumers suffer from limited information. Consequently, retailers strive to mitigate it through product images as a primary source of information, aiming to depict features accurately. This study examines the impact of visual features of clothing images on consumer purchase behaviors, focusing on the role of visual feature accuracy such as color and prints. Drawing upon the construal level theory and the two-stage process of online search, we categorize visual features into primary and secondary features and perform econometrics analyses. Key findings are: (1) consumers assess images based on primary and secondary features; (2) accuracy in primary features facilitates decision making, while accuracy in secondary features hinders it; (3) once a product enters a consideration set, image accuracy–whether primary or secondary–consistently increases purchase. These findings help online retailers enhance sales by strategically managing product image accuracy.

title: Social capital and online consumer review performance: The moderating role of platform- and peer-driven recognition
affiliations: Dongguk University, Cardiff University and Sungkyunkwan University

detail.title: Social capital and online consumer review performance: The moderating role of platform- and peer-driven recognition
detail.abstract: Online consumer review (OCR) platforms encourage reviewers to post many useful reviews, often relying on recognition systems to incentivize valuable contributions. However, these platform-driven mechanisms may overlook what reviewer-specific resources drive OCR performance. This study examines how three types of social capital (relational, structural, and cognitive) shape review quantity and quality, and how platform-driven (elite status) and peer-driven (fan count) recognition systems moderate the relationship between social capital and OCR performance. Based on social capital and self-determination theories, a theoretical model is developed. Analyzing metadata from 25,654 unique Yelp reviewers using covariance-based structural equation modeling, we find that relational social capital enhances both review quantity and quality, with stronger effects for highly recognized reviewers by platform (elite status) but weaker for those by peers (fan count). Structural social capital has no direct effect on OCR performance but becomes significant when coupled with platform-driven recognition. Cognitive social capital shows mixed effects, which are attenuated by peer-driven recognition. These findings offer actionable insights for online sellers and platform operators on how to identify, target, and cultivate well-performing reviewers to strengthen their brands.

title: Pre-Moderation in Online Brand Communities
affiliations: Tilburg University - Tilburg University School of Economics and Management

detail.title: Pre-Moderation in Online Brand Communities
detail.abstract: Firms operating online brand communities (OBCs) face a key tension: aligning user contributions with brand values without slowing the flow of fresh, engaging content. This study offers one of the first empirical examinations of how pre-moderation—moderating content before publication—affects user behavior. Leveraging a natural experiment in a large OBC dedicated to recipes for a kitchen appliance, I found that the policy reduced published recipes by 4.4 percent. This decline was driven primarily by inexperienced users, who published fewer recipes in oversaturated categories, and partly by experienced users, who were deterred by likely publication delays. The policy also lowered the novelty of published recipes, suggesting a narrowing of the acceptable solution space. However, user engagement with content, as measured by likes, remained largely unchanged. Together, these findings suggest that pre-moderation can inadvertently silence the periphery—deterring new or less-established contributors—and constrain creative freedom. For OBC operators, the results highlight a strategic trade-off: while pre-moderation can filter for quality and brand fit, it may also risk a drift toward homogeneity and disengagement of contributors.

title: Adoption of Generative Artificial Intelligence among Small Businesses - A Fuzzy Set Qualitative Comparative Analysis
affiliations: California State University, San Bernardino, Loyola Marymount University and Gachon University - College of Business and Economics

detail.title: Adoption of Generative Artificial Intelligence among Small Businesses - A Fuzzy Set Qualitative Comparative Analysis
detail.abstract: Given its early position in the adoption cycle, there is little systematic examination of the obstacles and resistance that could impede the widespread adoption of Gen AI in large or small businesses. In this paper, we explore how small businesses respond to the emergence of GAI focusing on the conditions that lead to its adoption by utilizing an inductive research approach. We utilized Fuzzy set Qualitative Comparative Analysis (fsQCA) and found the perception of the GAI among 121 small business owners and leaders to be a ‘core’ condition to adoption. This indicates that there exists a robust causal relationship between perception and adoption. In particular, we learned that the adoption of GAI was more likely among the small business owners when they saw it as an opportunity and felt a strong sense of urgency to do something with it. This research serves as one of the early attempts to analyze the adoption of GAI in small businesses. Besides, our research may be the first attempt that analyzes a broad base of small businesses representing many diverse industries. Second, this is one of the few papers that utilizes FsQCA to develop a more accurate and nuanced understanding of the factors that influenced GAI adoption among small businesses. Third and finally, our findings elucidate the potential utility of GAI for entrepreneurial firms and small businesses with limited technological backgrounds.

title: From Digital Twins to World Simulators: A Semantic Categorization Using Actor-Network Theory
affiliations: Independent and Independent

detail.title: From Digital Twins to World Simulators: A Semantic Categorization Using Actor-Network Theory
detail.abstract: This study offers a structured, actor-centric comparison of digital–physical systems by integrating Actor-Network Theory (ANT) into a semantic categorization framework. By analyzing Digital Twins, Cyber-Physical Systems (CPS), IoT, BIM, Simulation Systems, Synthetic Environments, the Metaverse, and World Simulation Models across five dimensions goal, physical–virtual interaction, connection to the physical world, physical model coupling, and data sources the paper clarifies how these systems differ in purpose, interaction modes, and real-world fidelity. Unlike traditional classifications emphasizing technical features, this approach highlights the socio-material assemblages through which these systems are constructed, maintained, and understood. Findings reveal a spectrum ranging from tightly coupled, real-time systems like digital twins and CPS, to speculative and generative models like world simulations that operate without physical referents. This distinction has practical and theoretical implications for conceptualizing, designing, and integrating emerging technologies. The framework contributes to Information Systems research by offering both a taxonomy and a lens to investigate hybrid agency and dynamic roles that technologies play in shaping future digital infrastructures and organizational ecosystems.

title: Image of the President in the Movie "The Way of the President: When the Stars Collide"
affiliations: Nazarbayev Intellectual School

detail.title: Image of the President in the Movie "The Way of the President: When the Stars Collide"
detail.abstract:
This study examines the cinematic portrayal of the First President of the Republic of Kazakhstan, Nursultan Nazarbayev, in the feature film “The Way of the President: When the Stars Collide.” The research aims to analyze how the director constructs the image of Nazarbayev through historical events, symbolic visual details, and narrative strategies that emphasize his personal qualities, leadership style, and role in shaping the destiny of independent Kazakhstan. Using a cultural-historical and film-analytical approach, the paper identifies the main artistic techniques employed in the movie to highlight Nazarbayev’s decisive character, moral strength, and political foresight. The analysis further explores the ways in which cinematic representation contributes to the formation of national memory and strengthens the perception of Nazarbayev as a central figure in Kazakhstan’s modern history. Special attention is paid to the symbolic use of metaphors such as “stars” as signs of destiny and collective progress, which reinforce the image of the President not only as a political leader but also as a figure deeply intertwined with the fate of the Kazakh nation.

The findings suggest that the film goes beyond a biographical retelling of events, functioning instead as a cultural narrative that seeks to inspire patriotism and pride among viewers. By depicting Nazarbayev’s struggles, decisions, and achievements, the movie reinforces his image as the architect of Kazakhstan’s independence and a unifying symbol for the people. Thus, the film serves as both an artistic interpretation and an instrument of historical reflection, merging national identity with the leader’s personal story.

title: Integrating Generative AI into Operations Research Education: Framework, Use Cases, and Ethical Reflections
affiliations: Catholic University of Lille - IÉSEG School of Management, Lille Campus and SAVILA EDUCATION

detail.title: Integrating Generative AI into Operations Research Education: Framework, Use Cases, and Ethical Reflections
detail.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is opening new opportunities to enhance the accessibility and personalization of Operations Research (OR) education. OR remains a challenging field to teach and learn, requiring students to progress from problem recognition to formal modeling, implementation, and communication. While GenAI has shown promise in other quantitative domains, its potential for OR pedagogy has yet to be systematically explored. This article proposes a conceptual framework that aligns the cognitive demands of OR education with the affordances of emerging GenAI technologies. We illustrate this framework through six use cases, ranging from lightweight supports such as audio-based learning and flashcards to more advanced approaches including customized tutors, retrieval-augmented generation, and agentic multi-agent systems. Each example is accompanied by implementation material to support adoption in practice. The article concludes by discussing ethical considerations and recommendations for responsible integration, highlighting how GenAI can complement rather than replace instructors in fostering engagement and durable learning in OR.

title: From GEO to AIVO: The Evolution of Digital Visibility Standards in the AI Search Era
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: From GEO to AIVO: The Evolution of Digital Visibility Standards in the AI Search Era
detail.abstract: Generative Engine Optimization (GEO) emerged in the early 2020s as a response to the rise of generative search engines and AI assistants. It provided organizations with a structured method to enhance visibility through citations, structured data, and user-generated content. While effective in bridging the gap between SEO and AI search, GEO is increasingly recognized as a legacy framework. The advent of large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude requires a successor framework: AI Visibility Optimization (AIVO). This paper provides a systematic analysis of the transition from SEO to AEO, GEO, and AIVO, and argues that AIVO is now the definitive standard for digital visibility in an AI-dominated search environment.

title: From Lebanon to Canada: The Role of Emotional Intelligence in Online Shopping Feedback
affiliations: UCAM Universidad Católica San Antonio de Murcia and UCAM Universidad Católica San Antonio de Murcia

detail.title: From Lebanon to Canada: The Role of Emotional Intelligence in Online Shopping Feedback
detail.abstract:
Background & Motivation:
As a frequent online shopper, looking for the best deals, and checking reviews myself for opinions and choices, my research is deeply entrenched in how true those reviews are, how genuine, relatable, and how the tone of those reviews impact brand image and purchase decisions. Managing a household abroad, juggling family and work obligations, and leading a life mediated by screens, emotional intelligence (EI) is crucial in digital communication. Some companies manage to empathize with customers by tackling their unpleasant relationships and turning them to loyal fans. This study tackles academic pursuit of emotional awareness for online platform success and personal reflection on a real-world phenomenon that impacts every online purchase. I am intrigued to look at the technical background of e-commerce and the human aspect for long vision success.

Research Objectives:
This paper critically looks at how emotional intelligence from consumers perspective and from e-retailers perspective has implication on ideas, taking decisions, and having faith in the reviews. The central research objectives are:

·       Analyze the role of emotional intelligence while understanding and answering reviews

·       Examine how feedback rooted in emotional intelligence impacts loyalty and satisfaction

·       Assess if such responses from sellers can manage negative comments and foster positive ones

Methodology: The study adopts a mixed-methods approach, combining:

·       A systematic literature review of EI and E-commers reviews impact

·       Case studies of EI-driven replies

·       Quantitative survey to bridge the gap between theory and lived experience.

Key Findings: The results indicate that those online consumers who have higher emotional intelligence have greater sensitivity when it comes to assessing reviews thus creating distinction between negative comments that are criticizing versus those who have given emotionally unhelpful feedback. Such consumers are highly likely to add value in their reviews and are on the lookout for responses in a timely manner from the sellers. For the vendors, businesses and websites that adopt a strategy that is emotionally intelligent with feedback that acknowledges emotions and share personalized feedback have higher customer retention and better reviews and ratings.

Personal Reflections: This research journey showcased the commonality of results between technology, emotion, and commerce. It is clearer now that emotional intelligence is not only a personal characteristic but a strategic tool for any encounter online between a consumer and a brand. Looking at emotional cues in reviews allows for a leeway to connect on a deep level and to change feedback into loyalty. Consumers are expecting more emotional communication in online transactions.

Conclusion & Contribution: This study enables better comprehension of emotional intelligence in e-commerce and customer experience management. As psychological insights have an impact on consumer behavior that should have an impact on practical strategies, the research closes a gap between academic inquiry and practical application. The framework enables emotionally intelligent feedback replies and staff to answer with empathy. Integrating emotional intelligence into online shopping leads to trust, and a more authentic online experience.

detail.abstract: Studies have found large differences in masks use during the pandemic. We found evidence that cultural tightness explains mask use differences and this association was more robust in tight situations like subways. In Study 1, we observed 23,551 people's actual mask use in public places around China. People wore masks more in tight situations, however, differences didn't extend to outdoor streets and public parks, where norms are looser. We replicated this finding using a dataset from 15,985 people across China. Finally, in a preregistered study we observed mask use with the removal of COVID-19 restrictions, people still wore masks more in tight situations like subways than in loose situations of parks. These findings suggest that norm tightness has a lasting association with people's health-protective behaviors, especially in tight situations. It provides insight into how different cultures might respond with future pandemics and in what situations people adopt health-protective behaviors.

title: Data Sovereignty and Privacy: A Chimera or Realistic Prospect in Aotearoa/New Zealand?
affiliations: University of Auckland Business School

detail.title: Data Sovereignty and Privacy: A Chimera or Realistic Prospect in Aotearoa/New Zealand?
detail.abstract: The recent trend for large global digital platforms, such as Amazon Web Services and Microsoft, to establish data centres in New Zealand has renewed the debate surrounding data sovereignty in the digital era. This article discusses the relevance of data privacy law for data sovereignty. It explores motivating factors underlying sovereignty claims, emerging cloud models in respect to access and control over data, and the benefits of localisation before examining the territorial as well as extraterritorial application of the Privacy Act 2020, and how these provisions might be applied to data clouds both in New Zealand and overseas. It draws on emerging organisational and technical solutions such as use of data trustees and encryption, to ensure sovereignty over data governance. Finally, it draws on overseas data privacy jurisprudence to demonstrate the current shortcomings of existing legislative provisions, before proposing solutions, including reform of the Privacy Act 2020.

title: A Strategic Peace Deal to End the War and Restore Ukrainian Sovereignty

detail.title: A Strategic Peace Deal to End the War and Restore Ukrainian Sovereignty
detail.abstract: This article proposes a paradigm shift in peacebuilding strategy for the Russia-Ukraine war and broader Eastern European stability. It argues that the prevailing Western approach-centered on sanctions, military deterrence, and diplomatic isolation-has failed to produce a durable resolution. Instead, it has entrenched authoritarian resilience and reinforced adversarial narratives. Drawing on behavioral political theory, the article introduces the concept of Authoritarian Loss Aversion, which posits that autocratic regimes resist compromise due to existential fears of regime collapse and loss of legitimacy. This psychological and institutional dynamic renders traditional coercive strategies counterproductive. In response, the article presents the Integration Paradigm: a strategic framework that replaces confrontation with structured inclusion. It rests on three interdependent pillars-Ukraine's permanent neutrality, phased territorial restoration, and conditional integration of Ukraine, Russia, and Belarus into the European Economic Area (EEA). This model reframes compromise as transformation, offering authoritarian regimes a face-saving exit from conflict while embedding them in legal and economic systems that incentivize reform. The article outlines policy recommendations for EU and international actors, including multilateral treaty design, transitional governance mechanisms, and generational engagement strategies. It also engages with ethical foundations rooted in Kantian cosmopolitanism and Just Peace Theory, emphasizing reconciliation, dignity, and shared prosperity. Ultimately, the Integration Paradigm offers a blueprint for durable peace-one that transforms adversaries into partners through strategic inclusion rather than punitive isolation.

detail.title: Defensive Specialization: Theory and Evidence from Mexico's Retail Sector

publicationDetails.detailsText: Cornell SC Johnson College of Business Research Paper

detail.abstract: Large companies are increasingly dominating the retail industry, casting doubt on the future of independent, local retailers. Is this the end of local retail as we know it? What product strategy should local stores follow to attenuate this negative impact? We show that, in response to increasing penetration of large chains, local retailers-especially smaller ones-optimally follow a strategy of defensive specialization. Intuitively, the arrival of large chains hurts all independent local stores, but it especially hurts general stores that sell multiple categories. Our empirical evidence, built on two large retail datasets from Mexico, confirms the predictions of the theoretical model: specialty stores are better able to cope with the shock of large-chain entry. Moreover, the entry of a large chain induces a shift toward greater specialization in the traditional retail sector, both through an increase in the absolute number and market share of specialty stores and through changes in the product offerings within local stores towards more specialization.

detail.abstract: Industry 5.0 represents a paradigm shift from the technology-driven orientation of Industry 4.0 toward a human-centric, sustainable, and resilient industrial ecosystem. This paper introduces the Systemic Innovation Blueprint (SIB), a multi-layered framework designed to operationalize the Industry 5.0 vision by embedding systemic innovation across industries, SMEs, public services, and community initiatives. detail.title: Industrial Policy in the Platform Economy
detail.abstract: Amid growing calls for stronger state involvement in the platform economy, there is still limited clarity on how such interventions should be designed and implemented. This paper examines how industrial policy can be adapted to platform-based markets, focusing on the direct state provision of platform services. Drawing on insights from platform studies, innovation economics, and political economy, I analyze the rationales, risks, and policy implications of this approach. I argue that direct provision is most justified in contexts of missing markets, platform dominance, pressing social needs, or strategic sectors. To navigate its challenges, I introduce two key concepts: platform capture, which warns of risks of state overreach, and ecosystem embeddedness, which underscores the importance of collaborative governance and stakeholder integration for adoption and resilience. The paper concludes by outlining a research agenda on how public platforms can complement broader industrial policy instruments in the digital economy.

title: Short Paper: Metrics for Innovation

detail.title: Short Paper: Metrics for Innovation
detail.abstract:
Innovation and creativity are essential for organizational success in today's competitive environment. However, these concepts are difficult to measure, and there is no single metric that can definitively indicate an organization's level of innovation.

Business metrics can be used to measure some aspects of innovation, but they should be interpreted with caution. Some metrics, such as the number of patents filed or the number of new products launched, can be good indicators of innovation, but they can also be misleading. For example, a company with many patents may not be very innovative if those patents are for incremental improvements to existing products.

Other metrics, such as the number of active products or the percentage of sales from new products, can be more useful indicators of innovation. These metrics can help to assess whether an organization is consistently introducing new products and services that are successful in the marketplace.

In addition to these traditional metrics, business intelligence (BI) can be used to measure innovation in more ways. BI can be used to track employee engagement, customer satisfaction, and social media mentions. These metrics can provide insights into how well an organization is creating and implementing innovative ideas.

detail.title: How Do Loyalty Programs Affect Multichannel Bookings? An Empirical Investigation
detail.abstract: With the increased market power of online travel agencies (OTAs), the hotel industry faces a new and important trade-off when working with OTAs: Potentially increasing sales at the expense of sizeable commission fees. In response, major hotel groups have turned to loyalty programs, offering discounts to loyalty members who book through their direct channels. Using a novel dataset from a franchisee of a major hotel group, we empirically investigate how loyalty discounts affect customers' booking channel choices. We utilize a quasi-natural experiment, based on an exogenous change in the loyalty discount for a subset of hotels in our dataset, to construct a difference-indifference model. We find that with a higher loyalty discount, consumers are more likely to choose booking directly as a loyalty member, less likely to choose booking directly as a non-member, and, surprisingly, equally likely to choose booking via OTA. Thus, a substitution effect only occurs within the direct channel, but not across channels. Our results indicate that discount-based loyalty programs, although widely used in the hospitality industry, do not have the intended effect of swaying customers from OTAs toward direct channels. Therefore, hotel groups may benefit from carefully reexamining their loyalty programs by considering their multichannel setting.

detail.title: HEAS: Hierarchical Evolutionary Agent Simulation Framework for Cross-Scale Modeling and Multi-Objective Search
detail.abstract: Hierarchical Evolutionary Agent Simulation (HEAS) is a Python framework that unifies layered agentbased modeling with evolutionary optimization and tournament evaluation in a single, reproducible workflow. HEAS represents models as hierarchies of lightweight processes ("streams") scheduled in deterministic layers that read and write a shared context, making cross-scale couplings explicit and auditable. A compact API and CLI-simulate, optimize, evaluate-expose single-and multiobjective evolution, PyTorch policy integration via parameter flattening/unflattening, and general tournament tooling with user-defined scoring and voting rules. The framework standardizes evaluation through uniform per-step and episode metrics, persists seeds, logbooks, and hall-of-fame archives, and provides plotting helpers for traces, Pareto fronts, and comparative outcomes, reducing glue code and improving comparability across studies. HEAS emphasizes separation of mechanism from orchestration, allowing exogenous drivers, endogenous agents, and aggregators to be composed and swapped without refactoring, while the same model can be used for forward simulation, optimization, or systematic comparison. We illustrate usage with two compact examples-an ecological system and an enterprise decision-making setting. HEAS offers a practical foundation for cross-disciplinary, multi-level inquiry, yielding reliable, reproducible results.

detail.abstract: This study investigates how country-level systemic readiness influences innovation in core and enabling renewable energy technologies, using panel data for 50 economies from 2000-2021. Readiness significantly enhances both innovation types, with results robust to alternative estimators addressing endogeneity, cross-sectional dependence, and serial correlation. Quantile regressions show that the marginal effect of readiness is stronger in the upper tail of the innovation distribution, where growth indicators such as GDP lose significance. Mediation analysis identifies socioeconomic vulnerability reduction and R&D investment as primary transmission channels, with renewable energy consumption marginally mediating enabling innovation. Panel Granger causality tests reveal a bidirectional dynamic relationship between core and enabling innovations, even after controlling for readiness and covariates, underscoring their coevolution. The results highlight the need for integrated policies targeting both innovation domains simultaneously to maximise the returns to systemic readiness.

detail.abstract: Transaction cost economics (TCE) predicts that asset specificity exposes suppliers to opportunism, but it largely treats buyer behavior as uniform. We propose that the personality of the customer's CEO shapes suppliers' perceptions of opportunism risk and, in turn, their willingness to make relationship-specific investments. Using CEO turnovers at customer firms as quasi-exogenous shocks, we link pre-constructed Big Five personality scores from unscripted earnings call Q&A to suppliers' R&D alignment in a difference-indifferences design. We find that incoming CEOs lower in openness, agreeableness, or extraversion lead suppliers to reduce alignment, whereas lower neuroticism (i.e., greater emotional stability) increases it. These effects are amplified when customers are less dominant in the dyad, as captured by relative size or sales. We also find that personality predicts relational structure, with more extraverted, open, and conscientious CEOs fostering longer, more extensive supplier ties. Our findings enrich TCE by incorporating behavioral heterogeneity in leaders and extend upper-echelons theory to interfirm coordination under contractual incompleteness.

detail.abstract: A large body of scholarship has documented evidence of racial and gender biases in large language models (LLMs). In this work, we examine three types of LLM biases in the context of caste and occupational identity in India through five studies. Our studies cover a comprehensive set of occupations in India and test for bias across all of India's districts. Our results provide four key insights. First, we find representation bias such that individuals from marginalized caste groups are significantly under-represented in LLM output compared to their share in India's working population. Third, the models also demonstrate selection bias with a higher probability of shortlisting resumes with names from dominant caste groups. Finally, we propose a training approach by which selection bias can be reduced in LLM shortlisting. Our work is highly relevant at a time when generative AI is becoming increasingly important in recruitment and hiring processes as a cost-saving measure.

detail.abstract:
When students are first introduced to the dominant federal legislation for tap water, the Safe Drinking Water Act of 1974 (SDWA), two things often stand out. The first is that SDWA is a technically complex statute. It establishes water standards for over 100 contaminants. The second is the huge number of water systems that are regulated. There are over 150,000public water systems scattered throughout the country. The vast majority of these public water systems (PWSs) are very small. So here’s the problem. Is it realistic to expect small PWSs to comply with SDWA’s highly technical requirements? Is it likely that the 120,000 PWSs with little funding and limited staffing are all in compliance with all the drinking water standards? At face value, it seems the answer has to be, “No and No.” 

This article provides the first comprehensive law review analysis of small PWSs and their compliance with SDWA. These small systems face steep technical, managerial, and financial barriers to meeting SDWA’s complex standards. Drawing on over two decades of public health, law, and policy scholarship, the article examines persistent patterns of noncompliance, especially in monitoring and reporting, and highlights how challenges are compounded in disadvantaged, rural, and minority communities. It reviews policy responses—including funding programs, variances, consolidation, and privatization—and assesses their limitations in addressing systemic shortfalls. With the recent adoption of stringent standards for PFAS “forever chemicals,” the burdens on small systems are poised to intensify.

detail.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to simulate human behavior, but common practices to use LLM-generated data are inefficient. Treating an LLM's output ("model choice") as a single data point underutilizes the information inherent to the probabilistic nature of LLMs. This paper introduces and formalizes "model belief," a measure derived from an LLM's token-level probabilities that captures the model's belief distribution over choice alternatives in a single generation run. The authors prove that model belief is asymptotically equivalent to the mean of model choices (a non-trivial property) but forms a more statistically efficient estimator, with lower variance and a faster convergence rate. Analogous properties are shown to hold for smooth functions of model belief and model choice often used in downstream applications. The authors demonstrate the performance of model belief through a demand estimation study, where an LLM simulates consumer responses to different prices. In practical settings with limited numbers of runs, model belief explains and predicts ground-truth model choice better than model choice itself, and reduces the computation needed to reach sufficiently accurate estimates by roughly a factor of 20. The findings support using model belief as the default measure to extract more information from LLM-generated data.

detail.title: Dialysis Clinic Patient Flow and Work Design
detail.abstract:
For 467,000 patients in the United States with advanced kidney failure, hemodialysis is a life-sustaining treatment. Approximately 7,600 outpatient dialysis clinics serve these patients, whose treatment costs over $25 billion annually. Each treatment involves a pre-treatment "put-on" task and a post-treatment "take-off" task performed by patient care technicians (PCTs). These frontline workers face intense, overlapping demands that can compromise patient safetyespecially infection control-and contribute to PCT burnout. We study how to jointly schedule PCTs and patients to reduce makespan and increase labor efficiency in dialysis clinic operations.

We first analyze the prevailing "push" approach, which starts put-on tasks for treatment as soon as a station is free. We then propose two alternatives: an "interlaced" scheme that staggers put-ons and takeoffs to reduce idle time, and a "tandem" scheme that pairs two PCTs-one specializing in put-ons, the other in takeoffs across twice as many stations. Under standard conditions, we derive closed-form expressions for each approach's completion time and show that interlacing finishes earliest with homogeneous treatment durations, while tandem configurations can lower labor per patient. We also incorporate heterogeneous treatment durations to show numerically that our insights are robust.

In contrast to the push-focused approach, these insights direct facility administrators' attention to what is most important for labor efficiency: minimizing the time that a station is unoccupied between successive patients. Due to the inefficiencies associated with the push approach, transitioning to an interlaced or tandem system with increased standard task times can alleviate workplace stress and promote patient safety without increasing labor costs. Specifically, dialysis clinic managers could move from the common 15/15-minute put-on/take-off scheduling standard to a 25/20-minute standard, thereby allotting PCTs 50% more time to complete tasks.

detail.abstract: In this paper we present the results of experiments and computational analyses of trading in decentralized markets with asymmetric information. We consider three trading configurations, namely the ring, the small-world, and the Erdös-Rényi random network, which allow us to introduce heterogeneity in nodes degree, centrality and clustering, while keeping the number of possible trading relationships fixed. We analyze how the prices of a traded risky asset and the profits of differently informed traders are affected by the distribution of the trading links, and by the location of the traders in the network. Experimental results show that learning is enhanced locally by clustering rather than degree, pointing to a learning dynamic driven by interdependent, successive trading events, rather than independent exposures to informed traders. By calibrating a behavioural agent-based model to the experimental data we are able to estimate the speed at which agents learn and to locate where information accumulates in the market. Interestingly, simulations indicate that proximity to the insiders leads to more information in regular networks but not so in random networks.

Specifically, the research examines respondents' views across six key constructs: Knowledge Access, Redefining Roles and Skills, Legal Research, Data Privacy, Software Development, and Augmented Productivity. The non-parametric Mann-Whitney U test was applied to assess statistically significant differences in perceptions based on gender. The findings indicate that for most constructs-including Knowledge Access (p = .327), Redefining Roles and Skills (p = .433), Legal Research (p = .756), Software Development (p = .227), and Augmented Productivity (p = .632)-there were no statistically significant differences in perception between male and female respondents. This suggests a general consensus across genders in recognizing the transformative potential of AI in these domains. However, a significant difference was observed in the Data Privacy construct (p = .025), indicating that gender influences how data privacy issues in AI applications are perceived. Female respondents reported slightly higher concerns compared to their male counterparts. The results support the conclusion that while gender does not significantly affect perceptions of AI in most work-related areas, it does play a role in shaping concerns around data privacy. These insights are valuable for developers, policymakers, and educators working to promote equitable and inclusive AI integration in professional settings. Understanding gender-specific concerns-especially in sensitive areas such as data privacy-can help tailor strategies for responsible AI adoption and ensure that technological advancements align with diverse user expectations and ethical standards. Further research is recommended to explore the underlying factors contributing to these gendered perceptions.

The organization from the course scenario has a traditional hierarchical structure. This means that there is a clear chain of command, with each employee reporting to a manager. This structure can be effective for tasks that are well-defined and predictable. However, it can be less effective for innovation, which often requires cross-functional collaboration and risk-taking.

Skunk Works, on the other hand, has a flatter structure. This means that there are fewer layers of management, and employees are encouraged to work together across functions. This structure can be more effective for innovation, as it allows for faster decision-making and more flexibility.

title: Buy Now, Regret Later"? A Review Of Instant Gratification And Post Purchase Dissonance In E-Commerce
affiliations: Maharaja Surajmal Institute, Vivekananda Institute of Professional Studies, , Delhi School of Business and Amity University Uttar Pradesh, India - Amity School of Business

detail.title: Buy Now, Regret Later"? A Review Of Instant Gratification And Post Purchase Dissonance In E-Commerce
detail.abstract: By including immediate gratification as a main motivator for online purchases, the fast growth of e-commerce has changed consumer behavior. This review looks at the psychological processes behind impulsive buying behavior and post-purchase dissonance-two connected phenomena becoming more and more common in digital markets. Driven by dopamine release and reinforced by persuasive UX/UI design, scarcity cues, and AI-powered personalization, instant gratification promotes fast decision-making by reducing cognitive friction. These actions are amplified by social commerce, influencer marketing, and gamified shopping venues that use FOMO-fear of missing out-and social validation systems. But the very elements that promote instant purchases also cause increased post-purchase conflict, a state of regret or dissatisfaction brought on by unmet expectations. Based on Festinger's Cognitive Dissonance Theory, this review looks at personal, product-related, contextual, and technical influences that exacerbate this emotional fallout, including price sensitivity, product complexity, urgency cues, and social pressures. The study reveals how gender, cultural norms, and social support networks affect the severity of regret, therefore influencing consumer reactions including returns, complaints, and bad reviews. Ecommerce systems use a dual strategy-maximizing conversions through urgency and personalization, while minimizing regret through clear return policies, proactive customer support, and loyalty programs. However, current research reveals critical gaps, including the lack of longitudinal studies on gratification-regret cycles, limited exploration of personality-technology interaction effects, insufficient understanding of emotional recovery post-return, and minimal attention to the ethics of persuasive digital design. This review provides a conceptual model for striking a balance between profit-driven urgency and consumer psychological well-being by combining ideas from behavioral economics, neuroscience, and digital marketing. The results ask e-commerce participants to implement design and policy measures that maintain consumer happiness beyond the point of sale, hence developing ethical, sustainable, and trust-based digital economy..

detail.abstract: Emergency Medical Services (EMS) is a life-saving entity, but the population density in the rural setting is often low, which is accompanied by a lack of infrastructure and geographic isolation. The present paper discusses the potential possibilities of such a development; how Location Intelligence (LI), the process of utilizing geospatial data and analytics might be used to streamline the effective response time of EMS in a rural community. Making a usage of Geographic Information Systems (GIS), up-to-date traffic rates, population dispersion, and past experiences with emergency response, the research learns about spatial patterns as well as pinch points that compromise the functioning of the EMS. To model the best locations of the ambulance stations, in order to leverage areas of high risk and other areas as alternatives to achieve their optimal locational strategies regarding high priorities, the datadriven approach to modeling is adopted. Finding indicates the implementation of LI tools may help decrease the time of response on average by the rearrangement of EMS resources in a strategic manner while enhancing directions in routes. The results highlight the revolutionary nature of geospatial analytics when it comes to maximizing the effectiveness of healthcare delivery in rural areas, and can be used by the policymakers, EMS planners, and public health actors interested in refining the outcomes of emergency response in low-income regions.

detail.abstract: We develop a clustering-based algorithm to detect loan applicants who submit multiple applications (“cross-applicants”) in a loan-level dataset without personal identifiers. A key innovation of our approach is a novel evaluation method that does not require labeled training data, allowing us to optimize the tuning parameters of our machine learning algorithm. By applying this methodology to Home Mortgage Disclosure Act (HMDA) data, we create a unique dataset that consolidates mortgage applications to the individual applicant level across the United States. Our preferred specification identifies cross-applicants with 92.3% precision.
